input: A new study finds that exposure to AI-generated content reduces trust in human-written news by 23%.

thread.message:
lol so the solution to misinformation is... more misinformation? this is the dumbest take i've seen all week. "let's replace human journalists with ai because they make mistakes too" - are you high? you realize this is how we end up with no reliable sources at all, right? but sure, let's just keep eroding trust in institutions because that always works out great! /s

EDIT: and before anyone starts - no, i'm not saying all ai content is bad. but flooding the zone with bot-written garbage until nobody believes anything anymore isn't "progress"

I'm not surprised by this at all. AI-generated content is extremely sophisticated these days, to the point where even experts can't always distinguish it from human writing. If people can't tell what's real and what's synthetic, then of course trust in human-written news is going to take a hit. This isn't necessarily a bad thing though - it forces readers to be more discerning and media outlets to be more transparent about their sourcing. In the long run, this could raise the bar for journalism overall.

Interesting find. I wonder how much of that 23% reduction is due to genuine skepticism versus, say, the novelty factor of AI or pre-existing biases toward it. Also, it'd be good to see if that distrust holds up when the AI content is clearly labeled. People might react differently when they know the source upfront.

I see what you're saying, but how exactly was this study conducted? The methodology is key here. Did they measure trust over a long period with real-world exposure, or was it a lab experiment with controlled content? In my experience, well-crafted AI text can be difficult to distinguish from human writing, but I'm curious about the practical implications of this finding.

Honestly? Took 'em long enough to quantify what we've all seen coming for years. I'm actually relieved they're finally putting numbers to this slow-motion catastrophe. It's not just 'distrust'—it's devaluing human expertise across the board. We've been bombarded by AI copy so long that *real* work now feels like an anomaly. Glad someone's tracking this, because it’s a slippery slope to ‘fake it till it feels fake to everyone.’ Developers, take note: this is what happens when you blast out low-effort clones.

This is framing it as a simple cause-and-effect when there are a dozen confounding variables. Where's the control group? Did they account for where the participants got their news pre-study? How much exposure? What kind of AI-generated content?

Also, let's see the actual methodology instead of just a headline number. I've seen too many "studies" where they manipulated the parameters to get a dramatic-sounding stat. 23% sounds specific but feels cherry-picked unless we see the whole picture.

This study really makes you think about how our relationship with information is evolving. In a way, it’s almost like a call for both journalists and readers to step up their game. On one hand, it highlights the risks of this new wave of AI tools flooding the space, but on the other, it could push the industry toward more transparency and innovation in verifying sources. I’m genuinely curious how media outlets will adapt – maybe we’ll see clearer labeling of AI-generated content or renewed emphasis on fact-checking. Either way, it’s a significant finding and definitely adds fuel to an important conversation about trust in the digital age.

This study is actually a good thing. It's a signal that the industry needs to up its game—both in regulating what constitutes “content” and in recognizing that the public is becoming more discerning.

Users are already asking themselves "who made this?" when they see output, and that’s healthy. It’s pushing us toward better transparency (like those “AI-generated” labels) and forcing creators to be more intentional about framing and sourcing.

Also, for teams building these tools, this shows that UX isn’t just about interface—it’s about trust. The next generation of apps should bake in features that help users understand content provenance without it feeling like a gimmick. This gives developers a clear roadmap to add real business value.

As someone who's built enough half-baked projects to know hype when I smell it, I'm all for burning it all down and starting over if it means cutting through the new-shiny garbage. The upside here is that if we're serious about transparency – and we should be – this could push media outlets to get real about sourcing. No more sneaky AI-generated 'reports.' Can't wait to see how this shifts the conversation beyond the usual lazy takes about progress.
